findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Verify that `summarize_for_isf`'s return type is changed to expose `_usage` (e.g. `(str, dict)`) and that this signature change is added to the Scope and Approach — the current single-string return makes the usage permanently unreachable by `pass1_isf`.

findings.finding: The plan asserts that `summarize_for_isf`'s summarizer call's usage 'is captured the same way and attributed to the ISF criterion,' but `summarize_for_isf` (passes.py:530-546) currently returns only `str(runner.run(req).get('text', ''))` — it discards the full result dict, so `_usage` is permanently unreachable by the caller (`pass1_isf`). For the plan's attribution to work, `summarize_for_isf` must also change its return type to expose the usage (e.g. return `(str, dict)`), but the plan neither names this signature change nor adds `summarize_for_isf` to the scope file list.

scenarios: ISF summarizer tokens are silently lost even though the plan claims they are captured; the per_call aggregate underreports ISF usage whenever summarization fires
A test asserting ISF summarizer usage is non-zero will always see zero
findings.suggested_fix: Add `summarize_for_isf` to Scope. Change its return to `(text, usage_dict)`, update `_linked_session_log` (or its caller) to unpack and thread the usage into the ISF call record.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the provenance and semantics of the `requests` field in the per-call record (e.g., 'always set to 1 — one record represents exactly one completed LLM call — and is copied from `_usage["requests"]` if present, else defaulted to 1') so the implementer has an unambiguous rule.

'the requests field count in full for each covered criterion' — implies requests can vary

findings.finding: The `requests` field in the per-call usage record is listed in the aggregation protocol ({criteria, requests, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens}) but its provenance and semantics are never defined: the plan simultaneously says 'one record IS one call' (implying requests is always 1) yet lists `requests` as a distinct field and says 'the requests field count in full for each covered criterion' (implying it can vary). An implementer cannot determine whether to hardcode 1, copy it from the runner's `_usage` dict verbatim, or compute it differently.
findings.location: Approach section, aggregation protocol paragraph: 'usage is recorded per CALL as {criteria: [ids the call covered], requests, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens}'
scenarios: Implementer sets requests=1 always; consumer code that reads the field for rate-limit accounting silently under-counts if the LLM client batches or retries internally.
Implementer copies requests from _usage verbatim; the field ends up with unexpected values that the per-criterion aggregation logic doesn't handle correctly.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to the aggregation protocol: 'The `requests` field is set to `_usage.get("requests", 1)` — for a single-turn call this is always 1, and the field exists for forward-compatibility with batch-API responses where a single runner.run call may represent multiple HTTP requests.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how the concurrent-futures collector handles futures that raise or return non-tuple values after the unpacking change — at minimum document that fu.result() exceptions are caught per-future (matching the existing graceful-skip behavior) and that a None/unexpected return degrades to ([], {}) rather than propagating.
evidence: Plan says: 'the concurrent-futures collector at pass1.py:490 changes from findings.extend(fu.result() or []) to unpacking: each future resolves to (findings_list, usage_records); the collector extends findings and appends the records'
The existing `or []` guard handled None/falsy returns silently; the plan does not state what replaces this guard in the new unpacking form
AC item 4 ('Missing _usage on any call degrades to zeros') covers the within-call case but not the future-raises / None-return case in the collector
findings.finding: The concurrent-futures collector change removes the existing `fu.result() or []` guard without specifying equivalent error handling for the new tuple-unpack form. If a future raises or returns an unexpected shape (e.g., None from an error path in pass1_chunk), the new `findings_list, usage_records = fu.result()` will raise a TypeError or propagate the future's exception rather than degrading gracefully — potentially aborting the entire batch collection rather than skipping the failed chunk.
findings.location: pass1.py:490 concurrent-futures collector, Approach section paragraph describing the collector change
scenarios: A single chunk's LLM call raises an unhandled exception inside pass1_chunk after the return-type change; the future resolves to an exception; the collector's tuple-unpack propagates it and aborts findings collection for all remaining chunks
pass1_chunk returns None on a rare error path; tuple unpacking raises TypeError and kills the collector loop
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the collector unpack in a try/except: `try: chunk_findings, chunk_usage = fu.result(); findings.extend(chunk_findings); usage_records.append(chunk_usage) except Exception as exc: logger.warning('chunk future failed, skipping: %s', exc)` — preserving the existing skip-on-error behavior while adding usage accumulation.

findings.finding: The plan's invariant 'retry usage is never discarded (billed is billed)' is unachievable for the context-limit-exception path via the current runner API: when pass1_with_ladder's batch call raises a context-limit exception, runner.run raises BEFORE executing `result['_usage'] = usage` (runner.py:543), so there is no _usage dict on the exception object and no return value to harvest. The plan specifies no mechanism (e.g., attaching partial usage to the exception, or a usage-capture callback in runner.run) to collect the failed attempt's billed tokens.
findings.location: Approach section: 'Ladder retries: every attempt pass1_with_ladder makes for a chunk — including escalation retries after a context-limit error — appends its own call record (billed is billed; retry usage is never discarded)'
findings.suggested_fix: In runner.run, attach the partial `usage` dict to the exception before re-raising (e.g. `exc.partial_usage = usage`), and update pass1_with_ladder's except blocks to read `getattr(exc, 'partial_usage', {})` and append a call record with those partial tokens.

findings.finding: The plan specifies a per-call usage record schema that includes a `llm_calls` field — `{criteria, llm_calls, requests, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens}` — but `runner._extract_usage` (runner.py:699-708), the sole source of the `_usage` dict, produces only `{input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens, requests}`. There is no `llm_calls` key in the runner's output; it would have to be a synthetic field added by the accumulator (always 1 per call record). The plan never acknowledges this derivation, treating `llm_calls` as if it already flows from the runner.
findings.location: Approach section — 'Aggregation protocol' / 'usage is recorded per CALL as {criteria: [ids...], llm_calls, requests, ...}'

findings.finding: The plan's 'Alternative rejected' section dismisses only the REBAR_USAGE_LOG JSONL path, but does not consider the existing OTel/Langfuse tracing infrastructure (tracing.py + Agent.instrument_all()) as prior art. When Langfuse is configured, pydantic-ai already emits per-LLM-call span data — including token usage — to Langfuse via the existing OTel provider. Tagging OTel spans with criterion IDs (a standard OTel pattern) is a direct alternative to the bespoke in-process accumulator this plan builds; the plan should either acknowledge this path and justify preferring in-process accumulation (e.g., always-on vs. opt-in keys, criterion tagging granularity, offline-reconstructability without Langfuse access) or show it was considered.
findings.location: Approach section — 'Alternative rejected' paragraph
scenarios: A reviewer or future maintainer discovers that Langfuse already holds per-call token data for configured deployments, and questions why a parallel in-process accumulator was added rather than enriching the existing OTel spans with criterion tags.
The team later adopts Langfuse more broadly and discovers duplicated token accounting between the sidecar's per_call records and Langfuse's span data, with no documented reconciliation strategy.
